topic: Fear of missing out keeps you checking
angle: While FoMO is strongly linked to problematic and social smartphone use, certain types of online interaction can actually mitigate feelings of loneliness and stress.
title: The Dual Nature of Connection

reveal.headline: Online interactions can reduce loneliness.
reveal.body: Specific types of online communication, such as one-to-one friendship and self-disclosure, can mitigate feelings of loneliness and stress.

explain.headline: The link between fear and use.
explain.body: Fear of missing out is most strongly related to problematic smartphone use. It may be part of social networking site addiction. However, the evidence shows mixed results regarding well-being.

matters.headline: The nuance of your screen time.
matters.body: That may be why your phone feels like a burden in some moments and a lifeline in others. The impact depends on the quality of the interaction.

example.headline: A late night message.
example.body: You sit in a dark room. You send a private message to a friend. You feel less alone for a moment before looking at the next notification.

claims.text: One-to-one communication, self-disclosure in the context of mutual online friendship, as well as positive and funny online experiences mitigated feelings of loneliness and stress.
claims.quote: In particular, one-to-one communication, self-disclosure in the context of mutual online friendship, as well as positive and funny online experiences mitigated feelings of loneliness and stress.

claims.text: Parasocial engagement is reliably linked to both enhanced well-being and problematic engagement.
claims.quote: Parasocial engagement functions as a psychological double-edged sword, reliably linked to both enhanced well-being and problematic engagement.

claims.text: Fear of missing out (FoMO) is most strongly related to both problematic smartphone use and social smartphone use compared to negative affect and fears of negative and positive evaluation.
claims.quote: Results demonstrated that FoMO was most strongly related to both problematic smartphone use and social smartphone use relative to negative affect and fears of negative and positive evaluation, and these relations held when controlling for age and gender.

verdict: The evidence shows a strong association between FoMO and problematic smartphone use, but also highlights that specific positive online behaviors can have beneficial mental health outcomes.
caveat: Several key studies are observational, meaning they show associations rather than proving that FoMO causes problematic smartphone use.
caption:
Fear of missing out is a primary driver of problematic smartphone use.

Research shows a strong association between FoMO and social media addiction, though several studies are observational. However, specific interactions like one-to-one communication can actually reduce stress.
